unit_label: Module D unit 6 (courseware unit 31): scale based regulation, NBFC governance, compliance function and CCO in NBFCs

facts.statement: Layers under scale based regulation (2025 Directions, paragraphs 8 to 15): the regulatory structure has four layers based on size, activity and perceived riskiness: NBFC-Base Layer (BL), Middle Layer (ML), Upper Layer (UL) and Top Layer (TL). The Base Layer comprises non-deposit taking NBFCs below asset size Rs 1,000 crore and NBFCs undertaking these activities: peer to peer lending platform (NBFC-P2P), account aggregator (NBFC-AA), non-operative financial holding company (NOFHC) and NBFCs not availing public funds and not having any customer interface (renamed Type I NBFC from 1 July 2026, after the cut-off). The Middle Layer comprises all deposit taking NBFCs irrespective of asset size, non-deposit taking NBFCs with asset size Rs 1,000 crore and above, and NBFCs undertaking these activities: standalone primary dealer (SPD), infrastructure debt fund NBFC (IDF-NBFC), core investment company (CIC), housing finance company (HFC) and infrastructure finance company (NBFC-IFC). The Top Layer is ideally empty and gets populated only if RBI considers there is a substantial increase in potential systemic risk from specific Upper Layer NBFCs, which then move to the Top Layer; Top Layer NBFCs are subject to a higher capital charge communicated at classification and intensive supervisory engagement. Activity based prescriptions: P2P, AA, NOFHC and NBFCs without public funds and customer interface always remain in the Base Layer; NBFC-D, CIC, NBFC-IFC and HFC are in the Middle Layer or the Upper Layer (not the Base Layer); SPD and IDF-NBFC always remain in the Middle Layer; the remaining NBFCs (NBFC-ICC, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-Factors and Mortgage Guarantee Companies) can lie in any layer depending on the scale based parameters. Regulations for lower layers apply automatically to higher layers unless stated otherwise.
facts.locator: RBI_NBFC_SBR_2025 paragraphs 8 to 15, 32 to 36; S01 printed pp. 657-658

facts.statement: Group classification and Upper Layer criteria (2025 Directions): NBFCs in a common group, or floated by a common set of promoters, are not viewed on a standalone basis; the total assets of all registered NBFCs in the group (including NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, NOFHC and NBFCs without public funds and customer interface) are consolidated to test the Middle Layer threshold; if consolidated assets are Rs 1,000 crore or above, each NBFC-ICC, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-Factor and Mortgage Guarantee Company in the group is classified in the Middle Layer, while NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA and similar Base-Layer-always categories stay in the Base Layer; statutory auditors certify the asset size (as on 31 March) of all NBFCs in the group every year; these group rules do not apply to Upper Layer classification. Once a non-deposit taking NBFC reaches asset size Rs 1,000 crore it is subject to Middle Layer regulation even if it later falls below on a given date, until its next audited balance sheet and a specific RBI dispensation. The Upper Layer, as amended by the Second Amendment Directions of 24 June 2026 (in force at the cut-off), consists of NBFCs with asset size of Rs 1,00,000 crore and above as per the latest audited balance sheet, identified annually by RBI as warranting enhanced regulation; the threshold is reviewed every three years. The courseware's earlier scoring methodology (top ten NBFCs by asset size always in the Upper Layer; top 50 by total exposure; 70 per cent quantitative and 30 per cent qualitative weights; supervisory judgement) was replaced and is not taught.
facts.locator: RBI_NBFC_SBR_2025 paragraphs 12, 17 to 24, 31; S01 printed p. 658

facts.statement: Transition path to the Upper Layer (2025 Directions, paragraphs 27 to 29): once an NBFC is identified for the Upper Layer and advised by RBI, within three months it puts in place a Board approved policy for adopting the enhanced framework and a plan for implementation; the Board ensures the stipulations are adhered to within a maximum of 24 months from the date of advice (the three months are included in the 24 months); calibrated increments to business may be allowed through supervisory engagement during the transition; the Board approved roadmap is submitted to RBI and is subject to supervisory review. An NBFC categorised as Upper Layer stays subject to enhanced regulation for at least five years from classification even if it does not meet the criteria in later years; it can move out only if it fails the criteria for five consecutive years. It may move out earlier if the move is a voluntary strategic readjustment of operations under a Board approved policy, but not if scaling down results from adverse situations specific to the NBFC and its deteriorating financial condition.
facts.locator: RBI_NBFC_SBR_2025 paragraphs 27 to 29; S01 printed p. 663

facts.statement: Net owned fund (NOF) requirements (2025 Directions, paragraphs 39 to 43): Rs 10 crore for NBFC-ICC, NBFC-MFI and NBFC-Factor to commence or carry on business; Rs 2 crore for NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA and NBFCs without public funds and customer interface; Rs 300 crore for NBFC-IFC and IDF-NBFC. Glide path for existing NBFC-ICC, NBFC-MFI (without a separate North East Region requirement at the end) and NBFC-Factor to reach Rs 10 crore: NBFC-ICC: Rs 2 crore currently, Rs 5 crore by 31 March 2025, Rs 10 crore by 31 March 2027; NBFC-MFI: Rs 5 crore currently (Rs 2 crore in the North East Region), Rs 7 crore by 31 March 2025 (Rs 5 crore in the North East Region), Rs 10 crore by 31 March 2027; NBFC-Factor: Rs 5 crore currently, Rs 7 crore by 31 March 2025, Rs 10 crore by 31 March 2027. NBFCs that fail to reach the prescribed level within the stipulated period are not eligible to hold a Certificate of Registration.

Other changes under SBR as the courseware presents them: the NPA classification norm moved to overdue for more than 90 days for all NBFCs with a glide path (more than 150 days overdue by 31 March 2024, more than 120 days by 31 March 2025, more than 90 days by 31 March 2026; not applicable to NBFCs already following the 90 days norm); at least one director must have experience of having worked in a bank or an NBFC; a ceiling of Rs 1 crore per borrower for financing subscription to an Initial Public Offer (NBFCs can set more conservative limits); NBFCs make a thorough internal assessment of capital need on the lines of ICAAP (Pillar 2); NBFC-UL maintain Common Equity Tier 1 of at least 9 per cent of risk weighted assets, are subject to a leverage ceiling and hold differential standard asset provisioning; concentration limits for NBFC-ML and UL are merged into single exposure limits of 25 per cent (single borrower) and 40 per cent (group of borrowers) of Tier I capital instead of the earlier owned fund based limits (NBFC-UL follow these until a Large Exposure Framework is in place); sensitive sector exposure (capital market and commercial real estate) is subject to Board approved internal limits; restrictions on loans to directors and their relatives and to senior officers; NBFC-UL put in place internal exposure limits for other important sectors; NBFCs with 10 or more branches adopt a core banking solution with a three year glide path from 1 October 2022.

Governance Directions 2025, applicability and basic requirements: NBFC-BL comply with Chapter III, NBFC-ML with Chapters II, III and IV and NBFC-UL with Chapters II to V. All NBFCs: at least one director with relevant experience of having worked in a bank or an NBFC; a Risk Management Committee (RMC) at Board or executive level, responsible for evaluating overall risks including liquidity risk and reporting to the Board; prior written permission of RBI for any change in management that results in a change in more than 30 per cent of the directors, excluding independent directors (not needed for directors re-elected on retirement by rotation), while RBI is still informed of changes. NBFC-ML and UL: a Board approved fit and proper policy for directors with continuing due diligence and a quarterly statement and MD and CEO certificate to RBI within 15 days of the quarter end; an Audit Committee of at least three Board members (treated as the Companies Act section 177 committee where required); a Nomination and Remuneration Committee; a Chief Risk Officer (CRO) for NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, who has direct reporting lines to the MD and CEO or the RMC, whom the RMC or Board meets without the MD and CEO at least quarterly if the CRO reports to the MD and CEO, who has no reporting relationship with business verticals or business targets and no dual hatting, and who is appointed for a fixed tenure and may be moved before its end only with Board approval; a CCO, sufficiently senior, with a Board approved policy on the CCO's role and responsibilities to promote a good compliance culture (paragraph 25); Key Managerial Personnel hold no office (including directorships) in any other NBFC-ML or NBFC-UL except a subsidiary, though they may be directors of NBFC-BL; an independent director sits on the Boards of not more than three NBFCs (ML or UL) at a time, and the Board ensures no conflict from that; a Board approved compensation policy covering fixed and variable pay and malus and clawback; a whistle blower mechanism for directors and employees; and Board approved internal guidelines on corporate governance published on the website. NBFC-UL additionally: a Board with a mix of qualifications and experience; reporting to supervisors if an independent director is removed or resigns before the normal tenure; and mandatory listing within three years of identification, with disclosure on the lines of a listed company before listing (a proviso exempts NBFC-UL fully owned and controlled by Government, inserted 24 June 2026).
facts.locator: RBI_NBFC_GOV_2025 paragraphs 3, 8 to 10, 12 to 14, 17 to 21, 25, 26 to 29, 38, 41 to 43; S01 printed pp. 661-662

facts.statement: Compliance function framework for NBFC-UL and NBFC-ML (RBI circular of 11 April 2022): applicable to all NBFC-UL and NBFC-ML (NBFC-BL continue under the existing guidelines); the Board approved policy and compliance function including a CCO were to be in place by 1 April 2023 (NBFC-UL) and 1 October 2023 (NBFC-ML); the circular is a set of minimum guidelines applied with proportionality. Compliance risk is the risk of legal or regulatory sanctions, material financial loss or loss of reputation an NBFC may suffer as a result of failure to comply with laws, regulations, rules and codes of conduct applicable to its activities. The Compliance Function ensures strict observance of all statutory and regulatory requirements, including standards of market conduct, managing conflict of interest, treating customers fairly and ensuring suitability of customer service. The Board or Board Committee ensures an appropriate compliance policy is put in place and implemented and prescribes the periodicity for review of compliance risk; the Senior Management carries out an exercise at least once a year to identify and assess the major compliance risk and formulates plans, submits reviews at the prescribed periodicity and a detailed annual review, and reports promptly on any material compliance failure while ensuring remedial or disciplinary action. The Compliance Function assists the Board and senior management in overseeing the implementation of the policy, has the central role in identifying the level of compliance risk (analysing risks in existing and new products and putting mitigants in place; the CCO is a member of the new product committee; all new products are intensively monitored for at least the first six months), monitors and tests compliance through sufficient and representative testing reported to senior management, periodically circulates instances of failures with preventive instructions, examines staff accountability for major failures, ensures compliance with RBI directions in letter and spirit in a time bound and sustainable manner (RBI expects all Risk Mitigation Plan and Monitorable Action Plan points to be complied with within timelines; unsatisfactory compliance may invite penal action), attends to directions of other regulators and brings discomfort conveyed by other regulators or action by other authorities to RBI's notice, and may serve as a reference point for staff queries. The CCO is the nodal point of contact between the NBFC and regulators and participates in structured or other regular discussions with RBI; compliance with RBI inspection reports is communicated to RBI through the office of the Compliance Function. Where separate departments look after different requirements they hold the prime responsibility for their areas, with overall oversight by the Compliance Function.
facts.locator: RBI_NBFC_CCO_2022 paragraphs 1 to 5; S01 printed pp. 664-665

facts.statement: Policy, structure and programme (RBI circular of 11 April 2022): the Board approved Compliance Policy spells out the compliance philosophy, expectations on compliance culture, structure and role of the compliance function, the role of the CCO, and processes for identifying, assessing, monitoring, managing and reporting compliance risk, and is reviewed at least once a year; it covers independence of the function and its right to disclose findings freely to senior management and the Board or Board Committee, regulatory and statutory requirements, a monitoring mechanism for compliance testing, reporting requirements including risk assessment and change in risk profile, the authority of the function to access information, a mechanism for disseminating regulatory prescriptions and updating operational manuals, and the Compliance Department's approval of all new processes and products before introduction. The Compliance Department is headed by the CCO; NBFCs may adopt their own structure but the function is independent, sufficiently resourced, with clearly specified responsibilities and periodic independent review. The annual compliance risk assessment and plan, carried out by senior management, covers at least compliance failures in the preceding year with losses and regulatory action and steps to avoid recurrence; all major regulatory guidelines issued during the year and steps taken; compliance with fair practices codes and standards of self-regulatory bodies and accounting standards; and progress in rectifying significant deficiencies and implementing recommendations from audits and RBI inspection reports. Authority: the CCO and function may communicate with any staff member and access all records and files needed, flowing from the policy. Dual hatting: the CCO is not given any responsibility with a conflict of interest, especially a business role, and generally is not a member of a committee that conflicts with the role (including purchases or sanctions committees), in which case the role is only advisory; compliance staff focus primarily on compliance but may be assigned other duties without conflict. Staffing: staff with basic qualifications and practical experience in business lines or audit and inspection, plus adequate staff with knowledge of statutory and regulatory prescriptions, law, accountancy, risk management and information technology, with appropriate succession planning. Internal audit: compliance risk is part of the internal audit risk assessment, the compliance function is subject to regular internal audit and the CCO is kept informed of compliance audit findings as feedback. Supervisory focus: compliance rigor is part of RBI's supervisory risk assessment.
facts.locator: RBI_NBFC_CCO_2022 paragraphs 6.A to 6.H; S01 printed pp. 665-667

facts.statement: Appointment and tenure of the CCO in NBFC-UL and NBFC-ML (RBI circular of 11 April 2022): tenure of a minimum fixed tenure of not less than 3 years, which the Board or Board Committee may relax by one year in exceptional cases provided succession planning is in place; transfer or removal before the end only in exceptional circumstances with the explicit prior approval of the Board or Board Committee after a well-defined and transparent internal administrative procedure; rank: a senior executive with a position not below two levels from the CEO, relaxable by one further level for NBFC-ML, and the CCO may be recruited from the market; skills: good understanding of the industry and risk management practices, knowledge of regulations and legal requirements, and sensitivity to supervisory expectations; stature: ability to exercise judgement independently and freedom and authority to interact with regulators directly; conduct: a clean track record and unquestionable integrity; selection through a well-defined process and recommendation of a committee constituted by the Board or Board Committee, with the Board or Board Committee taking the final decision; prior intimation to the Senior Supervisory Manager, Department of Supervision, RBI, before appointment, premature transfer, resignation, early retirement or removal, supported by a detailed profile and the fit and proper certification by the MD and CEO and the rationale for changes; reporting line: direct reporting lines to the MD and CEO and/or the Board or Board Committee; if the CCO reports to the MD and CEO the Board or Board Committee meets the CCO quarterly one-to-one without senior management (including the MD and CEO); no reporting relationship with business verticals; performance appraisal reviewed by the Board or Board Committee. Unlike the bank circular of 11 September 2020, the NBFC circular has no age limit and no minimum years of experience, but adds the clean track record condition and the tenure and rank relaxations. Board Committee means the Audit Committee of the Board where applicable.
facts.locator: RBI_NBFC_CCO_2022 paragraph 7 and footnote 3; S01 printed pp. 667-668

payload.title: The four layers of scale based regulation
payload.core_explanation_md:
NBFC regulation is built on **proportionality**: four layers by **size, activity and perceived riskiness**.

| Layer | Who is in it |
| --- | --- |
| **Base (BL)** | **Non-deposit taking NBFCs below Rs 1,000 crore**; **NBFC-P2P**, **NBFC-AA**, **NOFHC**; NBFCs **not availing public funds and with no customer interface** |
| **Middle (ML)** | **All deposit taking NBFCs** (any size); **non-deposit taking NBFCs with Rs 1,000 crore or more**; **SPD, IDF-NBFC, CIC, HFC, NBFC-IFC** |
| **Upper (UL)** | NBFCs **identified annually** by RBI for **enhanced regulation** (criterion in the next card) |
| **Top (TL)** | **Ideally empty**; filled only if RBI sees a **substantial rise in systemic risk** from an Upper Layer NBFC; **higher capital charge** and **intensive supervision** |

**Rules of thumb:** regulations for **lower layers also apply to higher layers** unless stated otherwise.

**Activity based placement:**

- **Always Base:** P2P, AA, NOFHC, NBFCs with no public funds and no customer interface.
- **Always Middle:** **SPD** and **IDF-NBFC**.
- **Middle or Upper (never Base):** **NBFC-D, CIC, NBFC-IFC, HFC**.
- **Any layer:** **ICC, MFI, Factor, Mortgage Guarantee Companies**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: From 1 July 2026 (after the cut-off) the no-public-funds category is renamed Type I NBFC; it is not taught here.

self_check.prompt_text: Which NBFCs always stay in the Middle Layer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Standalone primary dealers (SPD) and infrastructure debt fund NBFCs (IDF-NBFC).

payload.title: Group treatment and the Upper Layer criterion
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Groups are not viewed one by one.** NBFCs in a common group, or floated by a common set of promoters, have their **total assets added** (including NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, NOFHC and no-public-funds NBFCs) to test the **Rs 1,000 crore Middle Layer threshold**.

- If the **group total is Rs 1,000 crore or more**, each **NBFC-ICC, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-Factor and Mortgage Guarantee Company** in the group becomes **Middle Layer**.
- **P2P, AA and similar always-Base NBFCs stay in the Base Layer.**
- **Statutory auditors certify** the group's asset size (as on 31 March) **every year**.
- The group rule does **not** apply to **Upper Layer** classification.

**Staying in the Middle Layer:** once a non-deposit NBFC reaches **Rs 1,000 crore** it follows Middle Layer rules even if assets dip, until its **next audited balance sheet** and a specific RBI dispensation.

**Upper Layer (in force at the cut-off):** NBFCs with **asset size of Rs 1,00,000 crore or more** per the **latest audited balance sheet**, identified annually by RBI; the threshold is **reviewed every three years**. The courseware's older **scoring method** (top ten NBFCs, top 50 by exposure, 70:30 weights) was **replaced** by the amendment of **24 June 2026** and is **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A group of small NBFCs can therefore be regulated like a Middle Layer NBFC when their combined assets reach Rs 1,000 crore.

self_check.prompt_text: What asset size now identifies an Upper Layer NBFC?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Rs 1,00,000 crore or more as per the latest audited balance sheet.

payload.title: Classifying the NBFCs of a group
payload.core_explanation_md: A promoter group runs five registered NBFCs: an **NBFC-ICC** with assets of **Rs 400 crore**, an **NBFC-MFI** of **Rs 250 crore**, an **HFC** of **Rs 300 crore**, an **NBFC-P2P** of **Rs 40 crore** and an **NBFC-Factor** of **Rs 80 crore**. None takes deposits. Find the layer of each.

worked_steps.description: Add the assets of all registered NBFCs in the group (the P2P is included).
Compare with the Middle Layer threshold.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Group is at or above the threshold

worked_steps.description: The ICC, MFI and Factor take the Middle Layer.
The HFC is Middle Layer by activity (never Base).
The P2P platform is always Base.
Without the group rule the ICC (400), MFI (250) and Factor (80) would each be below 1,000.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Each would be Base Layer on its own

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Group assets Rs 1,070 crore; ICC, MFI, Factor and HFC are Middle Layer; the P2P platform is Base Layer

self_check.prompt_text: Would the answer change if the group total were Rs 990 crore?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes: the ICC, MFI and Factor would stay in the Base Layer; only the HFC would be Middle Layer.

payload.title: Moving into and out of the Upper Layer
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The five-year rule stops an NBFC from escaping enhanced regulation by trimming assets for a single year.

self_check.prompt_text: How long does an NBFC remain in the Upper Layer after classification even if it stops meeting the criteria?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least five years (exit only after failing the criteria for five consecutive years).

| **NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA**, and NBFCs with **no public funds and no customer interface** | **Rs 2 crore** |
| **NBFC-IFC and IDF-NBFC** | **Rs 300 crore** |

payload.title: Other changes under scale based regulation (courseware)
payload.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware; the NBFC prudential Directions were not retrieved, so none of these figures is tested).

- **NPA norm:** moved to **overdue for more than 90 days**, with a **glide path** (**150 days by March 2024**, **120 days by March 2025**, **90 days by March 2026**).
- **Board experience:** at least one director with **bank or NBFC experience**.
- **IPO funding:** ceiling of **Rs 1 crore per borrower**.
- **ICAAP:** thorough internal capital assessment on the lines of **Pillar 2**.
- **NBFC-UL:** **CET1 of at least 9%** of risk weighted assets, a **leverage ceiling**, **differential standard asset provisioning**.
- **Concentration:** single exposure limits based on **Tier I capital**: **25% single borrower, 40% group**.
- **Sensitive sector exposure:** Board limits on **capital market and commercial real estate**.
- **Restrictions on loans:** directors and relatives, senior officers.
- **Core banking solution** for NBFCs with **10 or more branches**.

payload.title: Governance requirements by layer (2025 Governance Directions)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Which chapters apply:** **BL: Chapter III**; **ML: Chapters II, III and IV**; **UL: Chapters II to V**.

**All NBFCs:**

- at least **one director with bank or NBFC experience**;
- a **Risk Management Committee** (Board or executive level) evaluating overall risk, **including liquidity risk**;
- **prior RBI permission** for a change in management changing **more than 30% of the directors** (**excluding independent directors**; not for directors re-elected by rotation).

**Middle and Upper Layers:**

| Requirement | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **Fit and proper policy** | Board approved; **quarterly statement** and **MD and CEO certificate** to RBI within **15 days** of quarter end |
| **Audit Committee** | **At least 3** Board members |
| **Nomination and Remuneration Committee** | As per the Companies Act (section 178) |
| **Chief Risk Officer** | For **asset size above Rs 5,000 crore**; independent: **direct line to MD and CEO or RMC**, **quarterly meeting without the MD** if reporting to the MD, **no business targets**, **no dual hatting**, **fixed tenure** |
| **Chief Compliance Officer** | **Sufficiently senior**, with a **Board approved policy** on the CCO's role |
| **KMP** | **No office in another NBFC-ML or UL** (subsidiary and NBFC-BL excepted) |
| **Independent director** | On **not more than three** ML or UL Boards |
| **Compensation** | **Board approved**: fixed and variable pay, **malus and clawback** |
| **Whistle blower mechanism** | For **directors and employees** |

**Upper Layer only:** a **competent mix** on the Board; **report removal or early resignation of an independent director**; **mandatory listing within three years** of identification (Government-owned and controlled Upper Layer NBFCs are exempt, from 24 June 2026).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The CRO rules mirror the CCO independence rules: no business targets, no dual hatting, a quarterly meeting without the MD.

payload.title: Can this person be the CCO of a Middle Layer NBFC?
payload.core_explanation_md: An **NBFC-ML** (not NBFC-UL) wants to appoint a candidate with a **clean track record** and a position **three levels below the CEO** (the CEO is level 0, the next officer level 1, and so on). The Board is considering a **tenure of 2 years** because the candidate retires soon, with a **succession plan** in place. Test the rank and the tenure, and say what would happen for an Upper Layer NBFC.

worked_steps.description: General rank rule: not below two levels from the CEO.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Level 2 is the lowest allowed for NBFC-UL

worked_steps.description: For NBFC-ML the requirement can be relaxed by one further level.

worked_steps.intermediate_result: Rank passes for NBFC-ML (it would fail for NBFC-UL)

worked_steps.description: Minimum fixed tenure is 3 years; the Board may relax by one year in exceptional cases with succession planning.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Minimum 2 years allowed in exceptional cases

worked_steps.description: A 2-year tenure with a succession plan meets the relaxed minimum.
Any removal before the term needs the Board's explicit prior approval in exceptional circumstances, with prior intimation to the Senior Supervisory Manager, Department of Supervision.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Eligible as CCO of an NBFC-ML (level 3 rank allowed, 2-year tenure allowed as an exceptional relaxation with succession planning); not eligible as CCO of an NBFC-UL because level 3 is below the rank limit

self_check.prompt_text: Could the Board relax the tenure to 1 year?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: the relaxation is only by one year, so the minimum is 2 years.

payload.title: Appointment, tenure and reporting line of the NBFC CCO
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Topic | NBFC rule (circular of 11 April 2022) | Bank rule (circular of 11 September 2020) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tenure** | **Minimum fixed 3 years**; Board may **relax by 1 year** in exceptional cases with **succession planning** | **Minimum fixed 3 years**; no relaxation |
| **Removal before term** | **Exceptional circumstances**, with **explicit prior Board or Board Committee approval** | Same, with **Board** approval |
| **Rank** | **Not below two levels from the CEO**; **NBFC-ML may be relaxed by one more level** | **Not below two levels from the CEO** |
| **Age and experience** | **No age limit and no minimum years** stated | **Age up to 55**; **15 years of experience, 5 in audit, finance, compliance, legal or risk** |
| **Conduct** | **Clean track record and unquestionable integrity** | **No vigilance case or adverse RBI observation pending** |
| **Skills and stature** | Understanding of industry and risk, knowledge of regulation, **independent judgement**, freedom to **deal with regulators** | Similar |
| **Selection** | **Board-constituted committee** recommends; **Board decides** | **Senior executive-level committee** recommends; **Board decides** |
| **Prior intimation** | **Senior Supervisory Manager, DoS**, before **appointment, premature transfer, resignation, early retirement or removal**, with **profile and MD and CEO fit and proper certificate** | **DoS, RBI Central Office**, before **appointment, premature transfer or removal** |
| **Reporting line** | **MD and CEO and/or Board or Board Committee**; if the MD and CEO, the **Board or Committee meets the CCO quarterly one-to-one without senior management**; **no business verticals**; **appraisal reviewed by Board or Committee** | Same, with the **ACB** |

**Board Committee** means the **Audit Committee of the Board** where applicable.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 2025 Governance Directions add only the headline rule: appoint a sufficiently senior CCO and have a Board policy on the CCO's role.

self_check.prompt_text: Does the NBFC circular set an upper age limit for the CCO?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; unlike the bank circular, it states no age limit.

payload.stem_md: Under scale based regulation, the regulatory structure for NBFCs has

options.text_md: Four layers: Base, Middle, Upper and Top
options.explanation_md: Scale based regulation sorts NBFCs into four layers: Base, Middle, Upper and Top, by size, activity and perceived risk.
Two layers of bank and non-bank ignore the scale and activity tiers.

options.text_md: Three layers: small, medium and large only
options.explanation_md: Three layers of small, medium and large omit the Top Layer and the Upper Layer wording.
Five layers is more than the four the Directions create.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Scale based regulation sorts NBFCs into four layers: Base, Middle, Upper and Top, by size, activity and perceived risk.

payload.stem_md: Which NBFCs are in the Middle Layer irrespective of asset size?

options.explanation_md: NBFC-ICCs can be Base, Middle or Upper depending on size.
All deposit taking NBFCs are Middle Layer whatever their asset size, because deposits bring public risk.
NBFC-P2P platforms always stay in the Base Layer.

options.explanation_md: A maximum age of 55 is the bank rule.

options.text_md: A requirement of 15 years of experience
options.explanation_md: 15 years of experience is the bank rule.
The NBFC circular does have a tenure rule.

options.text_md: No age limit and no minimum years of experience for the CCO
options.explanation_md: The NBFC circular has no age limit or minimum experience, unlike the bank circular.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The NBFC circular has no age limit or minimum experience, unlike the bank circular.

payload.stem_md: The CCO of an NBFC may be transferred or removed before completion of the tenure only

options.text_md: In exceptional circumstances with the explicit prior approval of the Board or Board Committee
options.explanation_md: Removal before tenure needs exceptional circumstances and explicit prior Board approval.
The MD's discretion alone is not enough.

options.text_md: At the request of a business head
options.explanation_md: A business head's request is not a ground.
Removal at any time would defeat the fixed tenure.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Removal before tenure needs exceptional circumstances and explicit prior Board approval.

payload.stem_md: A group has five registered NBFCs with assets of Rs 400 crore, Rs 250 crore, Rs 300 crore, Rs 40 crore and Rs 80 crore. What is the group's consolidated asset size (Rs crore) for the Middle Layer test?
An existing NBFC-ICC has a net owned fund of Rs 2 crore. By how many Rs crore must it increase the NOF to meet the final requirement?
An NBFC-MFI in the North East Region has a net owned fund of Rs 2 crore. By how many Rs crore must it increase the NOF by 31 March 2025 under the glide path?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Interim requirement Rs 5 crore: 5 - 2 = 3.

payload.stem_md: An NBFC has 12 directors who are not independent directors. What is the smallest whole number of such directors whose change triggers the need for prior RBI permission (change in more than 30 per cent)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: 30% of 12 = 3.6; more than 3.6 means at least 4.

worked_solution_steps.description: Smallest whole number above the threshold.

unresolved: The layer structure, categorisation, group consolidation, transition path and NOF requirements are taught from the 2025 Registration, Exemptions and SBR Directions (RBI_NBFC_SBR_2025; retrieved text is the version updated as on 1 July 2026). Only provisions in force at 30 June 2026 are taught. The Second Amendment Directions of 24 June 2026 (effective on issuance, before the cut-off) replaced the courseware's Upper Layer scoring methodology (top ten NBFCs, top 50 by exposure, 70 and 30 per cent weights) with an asset size threshold of Rs 1,00,000 crore, reviewed every three years; the old methodology is not taught. The Amendment Directions of 29 April 2026 (effective 1 July 2026, after the cut-off) rename the Base Layer category as Type I NBFC and are not taught.

The governance requirements are taught from the 2025 Governance Directions (RBI_NBFC_GOV_2025, updated as on 24 June 2026), which repealed the earlier governance instructions the courseware cites. The retrieved page shows paragraph 25 (CCO) requiring only the appointment of a sufficiently senior CCO and a Board-approved policy; the detailed framework (tenure, rank, reporting line and so on) is taught from the RBI circular of 11 April 2022 (RBI_NBFC_CCO_2022). Whether that circular was withdrawn or replaced before 30 June 2026 could not be verified (the bank equivalent was repealed only by Directions dated 31 July 2026); secondary reports mention separate Compliance Function Directions in 2026, not retrieved.

The courseware's other SBR changes (the 90 days NPA norm and its glide path, the Rs 1 crore IPO funding ceiling, ICAAP, 9 per cent common equity tier 1 and leverage for NBFC-UL, differential standard asset provisioning, the Tier 1 based concentration limits of 25 and 40 per cent, sensitive sector exposure and restrictions on loans, the Large Exposure Framework, the core banking solution requirement and the treatment of Government owned NBFCs) are the courseware's account (needs_review); the NBFC prudential Directions were not retrieved and these are not tested as figures.
The courseware text on NBFCs not availing public funds and having no customer interface reflects the pre-1 July 2026 wording; the 2026 Type I NBFC rename is after the cut-off.
